surfaces.part: moss cap on top of head
stone face (brow, nose, mouth/teeth), seen face-on

answer.evidence: The object is a round head drawn face-on, with the brow, nose and mouth seen from the front. The silhouette widens smoothly from 7px at row 2 to 27px at rows 16-18, then narrows to 14px at row 27. It is a single rounded blob outline, not a cap and shaft. The mossy green rows 2-6 are a patch on the upper edge of the head. They have no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no ellipse width profile, so they do not read as a horizontal surface. The scan shows only vertical face features (cream face, dark brow and mouth bands, grey shaded right half). No top plane is visible, so the drawing is a front elevation, not three-quarter. It is a single lying object, so it fits loosely as debris.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone head with moss on top, about 1.5 tiles across. It has 10 visible tones per tile, close to prop-hedge (9) and below the well (20) and cheese stall (17). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no large flat fills. The stone face has roughly 4 lightness steps: a highlight, a light, a mid and a dark tone for the eyes, mouth and cheek shadows. The moss cap has about 3 greens with little clump variation. Dark edge pixels are 30% neutral, so the outline is partly neutral and partly tinted. It reads as a darker grey-green line around the whole silhouette rather than a clearly material-matched tone, which gives a mild sticker look. The stone surface has few pits, cracks or per-stone dots, so the grain is thinner than the well's stonework and the stall's detail. It is clean and readable, but a careful artist would still see it as a little flatter and simpler than the best references, so I fail it on the 'when in doubt' rule.

answer.evidence: The silhouette is a rounded blob that widens from 7 px at row 2 to 27 px at rows 16-18 and narrows again to 14 px at row 27. It is the outline of a face drawn flat to the viewer, with brows, nose, closed eyes and a toothy mouth. Column x=15 shows only face tones (rows 7-14 light, rows 15-21 dark features), and column x=22 shows the shaded right half. There is no band ending in a front-edge line and no eave shadow. The only green rows (2-6) are moss, which counts as decor. The head is a face-on elevation with a mossy rim at the top, not a surface seen from above. It is a single object, not scattered pieces, but a fallen head is plausible as debris.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has about 5 lightness steps on the stone (highlight, light, mid, shadow, deep crevice) and about 3 greens on the moss cap. The facial planes, brow, cheek and mouth are modelled by value rather than outlined. Visible tones per tile are 10, level with prop-hedge (9) and below the well (20) and stall (17). This is a tinted material-tone outline, not a uniform black sticker line. Texture is moderate: moss clumps and stone speckle are present, but with only 15 total colours it is a little less grainy than the well or stall. It would sit acceptably next to the hedge and bench references.

answer.evidence: The object is a statue head seen face-on, drawn as a round silhouette with brow, nose and teeth on a vertical face. The moss at rows 2-6 is the crown, but it is a rounded outline with no front-edge line, eave shadow or ellipse. The width grows steadily from 7 to 27 and then shrinks, which is a sphere outline and not a distinct top plane. The face is vertical, so it reads as a front elevation. The kind is debris, and a single large head is a loose fit for scattered debris, but it is plausible as fallen rubble.

Only 30% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, and the face and moss separate mostly by value. It measures 10 visible tones per tile against 9 for the hedge, which is the closest reference in size and kind. Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no flat fills. Grain and speckle are lighter than on the hedge or well, which is why density is only slightly lower and texture is 'some' and not 'rich'. A careful artist would accept it next to the references.
